newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen ruling party poised to make major poll gains.
newsitem.headline: Yemen ruling party poised to make major poll gains.

text.p: Yemen's ruling party is expected to emerge with a large majority while its Islamist junior coalition partner could lose ground in results from Sunday's parliamentary elections, Western diplomats said on Tuesday.
Independents appeared poised to make strong gains in the ballot, which was overshadowed by shootings in which nine died and allegations of irregularities, they said.
A Supreme Election Committee official told Reuters that in counting so far, the General People's Congress (GPC) of President Ali Abdullah Saleh had won 57 seats in 83 constituencies.
Its coalition partner, the Islah, clinched 10 and independents took the rest. The election was for 301 seats in the national assembly.

In united Yemen's first elections in 1993, the GPC won 123 seats in parliament followed by Islah with 62 and the Yemen Socialist Party (YSP), 56. Independents won 47 seats while the rest went to Baathist and Nasserite parties.
Officials said first results would be announced by around 6 p.m. (1500 GMT).

The announcement gave no reason for the second postponment in two days, but officials said votes were still being counted in a process slowed down by huge voter turnout. They expected full results by Thursday.
Officials had said initial results would be unveiled by midday on Tuesday (0900 GMT) after a one-day delay.
Western diplomats and election observers said Islah could lose ground to the GPC, apparently because its ministers had failed to deliver many essential day-to-day services.

The Islamists hold socially sensitive portfolios such as electricity, health and water in one of the Arab world's poorest countries. The GPC controls the key ministries of defence, finance, interior and foreign affairs.
"Some Islah candidates were even defeated in their traditional strongholds," said one analyst.
"The GPC will win, more independents could be in and the Islah could lose some seats," said a Western diplomat. "The Islah portfolio has many political minefields."
Yemen is suffering from high unemployment and inflation and much of its hard-pressed population of 16 million fears further economic austerity.
Parliamentary speaker Sheikh Abdullah bin Hussein al-Ahmar of the Islah Party accused some ruling party members of hampering the count in many constituencies.
But deputy prime minister and GPC secretary-general Abdul-Karim al-Iryani denied the charges.

Ahmar insisted at a news conference in his home town of Khamir outside Sanaa late on Monday that the announcement of first results was delayed because some GPC members, local officials and candidates wanted vote-counting to be done in military camps instead of designated polling stations.
"The results are late because the GPC is hampering counting in many constituencies," he said.
"This is a violation of the law. It is evidence of bad intentions...We will not accept the transfer of ballot boxes."
An independent election monitoring group also dismissed Ahmar's remarks, but said two boxes might have been removed.
Turnout was officially put at 80 percent although international monitors believed it was closer to 60 percent.

The YSP, the main opposition group -- some of whose former leaders launched the separatist campaign that sparked civil war -- and three others boycotted the polls, alleging irregularities. The government denied the charges.

Officials said voting would be repeated in a constituency in Dhamar, 100 km (60 miles) south of Sanaa, after voters refused to cast ballots because the symbol of their candidate was missing due to an administrative error. They gave no new date.
